passage:
Monday. Akash sat on his sister Jahnavi's balcony floor and told her about the painkillers: a year of taking them long after his back had healed, lying to doctors, the gold bangle of Dadi's he had pawned. Jahnavi's first feeling was fury. Her second was guilt: she had noticed him getting thinner and said nothing. Underneath both was a strange relief. At last, it had a name.
Friday. At the family session at the de-addiction centre, the counsellor told them, "This is a health condition that changes the brain, not a sign that Akash is a bad person." Jahnavi found herself crying, half from anger and half from something loosening.
Three weeks later. She went alone to a Saturday group for families of people in recovery. A woman there said she had spent a year hating herself for her son's addiction. Jahnavi nodded hard. Walking home, she noticed she hadn't rehearsed an argument with Akash all day.

qa.q: What did the counsellor tell the family at the Friday session?
qa.a: "This is a health condition that changes the brain, not a sign that Akash is a bad person."

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Jahnavi have on Monday, and why?
qa.a: Fury at the lies, guilt for noticing him getting thinner and saying nothing, and relief that the problem finally had a name.

qa.q: How did the family group help Jahnavi stay steady?
qa.a: Hearing another family member's guilt made her feel less alone, and by the walk home she had stopped rehearsing arguments with Akash.

qa.q: What might Akash have felt telling his sister on the balcony floor?
qa.a: Akash was likely frightened and ashamed, confessing a year of lies and Dadi's pawned bangle, unsure whether she would turn away 🤍.

grounding: Shows a sister hearing about her brother's addiction with anger, guilt and relief, then steadied by learning it is a health problem and joining a family group.

passage:
Aparna, come, sit. Since your brother Vinod told you everything yesterday, you've had that face, and your Rukmini Chithi knows it. I wore it once.
I was twenty-four when my Appa sat us down one Sunday and said he had been drinking in secret for years, and that the shop debts were because of it. I was so angry I couldn't breathe. Then guilty, because I had laughed off his shaking hands. And under it, a terrible relief, because finally our house's strange silences made sense.
I thought feeling all three at once meant something was wrong with me. The doctor at the de-addiction ward told Amma and me that addiction is an illness, not a weakness of character. I didn't believe him at first.
What saved me was a group for families that met in a church hall behind the bus stand. There I learned I could be angry and still stand by Appa.
You don't have to choose one feeling, kanna.

qa.q: Where did the group for families meet?
qa.a: In a church hall behind the bus stand.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini think something was wrong with her at twenty-four?
qa.a: She felt anger, guilt and relief all at once and believed that feeling all three together meant something was wrong with her.

qa.q: What helped Rukmini stay steady, and what could Aparna take from it?
qa.a: Learning from the doctor that addiction is an illness, and joining the families' group; Aparna could look for similar support and allow mixed feelings without choosing one.

qa.q: What might Vinod be going through after telling Aparna everything?
qa.a: Vinod may be anxious about how Aparna will react, hoping that honesty won't cost him the family's support.

grounding: Illustrates, through an aunt's memory, a family member's mixed anger, guilt and relief on hearing the truth, and the help of learning addiction is an illness and joining a family group.

passage:
The hospital corridor was dim; the power had gone and only the emergency lights glowed. Elizabeth sat on a plastic chair beside her daughter-in-law, Jasleen. Her son Neil had just told them the truth: he'd been addicted to painkillers for a year, and tonight's collapse wasn't "just stress".
Elizabeth felt a flash of anger. How could he lie to us? Then guilt. How did I not see it? And underneath, strangely, relief. At least now they knew.
Jasleen was crying quietly. A nurse stopped and handed them a leaflet: a family support group, Tuesdays, and a line that read, "Addiction is a health condition, not a moral failure."
Elizabeth read it twice and held Jasleen's hand.

qa.q: When does the family support group meet?
qa.a: On Tuesdays.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Elizabeth have after hearing the truth?
qa.a: She felt anger at Neil's lies, guilt for not noticing, and relief that the truth was out.

qa.q: What could help Elizabeth and Jasleen stay steady now?
qa.a: Going to the family support group and learning that addiction is a health condition, not a moral failure.

qa.q: What is it like for Jasleen in the corridor?
qa.a: Jasleen is crying quietly, likely shocked and heartbroken, and needs support herself.

grounding: Shows a mother hearing her son's addiction truth with anger, guilt and relief together, and finding a family support group.

passage:
When her brother Abhinav told the family about his gambling debts and addiction, Parul was furious. She'd lent him money twice. She'd defended him to their parents.
That night in the Mumbai flat, she lay awake, angry, then guilty. Should she have seen it? Then, strangely, relieved. The lies were finally over.
The counsellor at the de-addiction centre suggested the family come to a session. Parul went, arms folded. The counsellor explained that addiction changes the brain, that it's a medical condition, not a lack of love or morals.
Afterwards Parul joined a family group that met on Saturdays. For the first time, she talked about her own anger without feeling like a bad sister.

qa.q: How many times had Parul lent Abhinav money?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What feelings did Parul have that first night?
qa.a: She felt angry, then guilty for not seeing it, then relieved that the lies were over.

qa.q: What helped Parul stay steady?
qa.a: Learning at the counselling session that addiction is a health problem, and joining a family group for her own feelings.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel knowing Parul came to the session?
qa.a: Abhinav may feel ashamed but grateful and less alone, seeing his sister show up.

grounding: Shows a sister feeling anger, guilt and relief on hearing her brother's addiction, and finding steadiness in counselling and a family group.

passage:
"Swati, I have to tell you something. I've been drinking in secret for a year. I'm going into a programme on Monday."
"A year? Chinmay, a YEAR?"
"I know."
"I asked you so many times!" Swati's voice shook. "And I believed you. I feel so stupid."
"You're not stupid. I hid it well."
She sat down. "Why didn't I see it?"
"It's not your fault."
A long silence. Then, quietly: "I'm angry. And I'm... relieved? Is that awful?"
"No. The doctor said families feel everything at once."
"Does the programme have something for me?"
"There's a family group on Thursdays."
"Then I'm going."

qa.q: When is the family group?
qa.a: On Thursdays.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when she said "Is that awful?"
qa.a: Swati felt angry and also relieved, and confused about having both feelings at once.

qa.q: What choice at the end will help Swati stay steady?
qa.a: Going to the family group on Thursdays, so Swati gets support too.

qa.q: What might Chinmay be experiencing as Swati reacts?
qa.a: Chinmay is probably ashamed and anxious, but trying to take responsibility and reassure Swati.

grounding: Shows a partner hearing about hidden drinking with anger, guilt and relief together, and choosing support for the family too.

passage: The night Ojas told us, I was angry first. Four years of excuses, the missing gold chain, the lies about night shifts, and I had defended him to our parents every single time. Then guilt came right behind it: I'm his elder sister, I lived with him, how did I not see? And under both, strangely, relief. At least now it had a name. The counsellor at the de-addiction centre met our family on Saturday and said something I keep repeating to myself: "Dolma, this is an illness that can be treated, not a character flaw, and families need support too." So now I go to a family group on Wednesdays. Some weeks I still feel furious. But I no longer carry all of it alone, and when Ojas calls, I can answer without my voice shaking.

qa.q: On which day does Dolma go to the family group?
qa.a: On Wednesdays.

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Dolma have the night Ojas told the family?
qa.a: Dolma felt angry, then guilty for not seeing it, and underneath both, relieved that it finally had a name.

qa.q: What has helped Dolma stay steady?
qa.a: Learning that the addiction is an illness that can be treated, not a character flaw, and joining a family group for support.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ojas when Dolma answers calmly?
qa.a: Ojas may feel less judged and more hopeful, hearing a steady voice instead of anger.

grounding: Shows a family member hearing the truth with anger, guilt and relief at once, then steadied by learning it is a health problem and getting support.
